newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Canada tycoon Munk to expand in Central Europe.
newsitem.headline: Canada tycoon Munk to expand in Central Europe.

text.p: Canadian Peter Munk on Friday signalled his intention to expand rapidly into central Europe with the opening in Budapest of the region's largest shopping mall.

"With our exceptional financial strength, strategic vision and real estate expertise (the real estate group) Trizec Hahn is now pursuing an aggressive growth strategy in Central Europe," Munk said in his opening speech.

The mall, Polus Center, has been backed by Hungarian and Canadian investors, grouping around Munk and including another Hungarian-born Canadian, Andrew Sarlos and a native Hungarian businessman, Sandor Demjan.
Munk controls Canada's Barrick Gold Corporation, and North American real estate firm Trizec Hahn, both of which have a strategy of rapid global expansion.
The 56,000-square-metre retail and entertainment centre was built at a cost of $120 million in only 344 days, which the investors described as a world record.

The constructors of Polus plan to build some 25 malls in central Europe over the next seven years, exploiting changing customer habits in a region where only three percent of retail trade goes through shopping centres -- compared to 50 percent in western countries and 70 percent in the U.S.
Demjan told reporters earlier on Friday that the plans, which are worth some $3 billion, also include the construction of modern office buildings and industrial parks in the region.
Earlier this year, Munk's companies took part in the construction of an industrial park on the outskirts of Berlin, and Hungary's first modern banking office centre in Budapest,
The projects, together with Polus Center, will serve as prototypes for further expansion in the region, Demjan said.

Despite the new atmosphere of the Polus, with its ice-rink, multiplex cinema, restaurants, banks, shops and internal spaces imitating a XIX. century town on the American prairie, the investors are convinced that the mall will have a strong appeal for Hungarians.

"Hungarian shops are not modern, transport and storing cost much," Demjan told a news conference on Friday, explaining why Polus will be cheaper than smaller shops. "At a size like (Polus) costs can be cut by 10 percent."
"A revolution is going on in trade (in the region)," he added. "Traders who do not set up in these shopping centers will be in a difficult situation."

Munk told Reuters that Trizec Hahn, which was set on a strong growth pattern, had identified the Central European area as one of the three geographical priority areas where the economic and the political scene was stable, and where there was demographic growth and rapid economic development.
"These are the Southeast Asia corridor, countries in Latin America like Chile, Argentina, Bolivia and Peru, and the Central European countries," he said.
